case.description: Full-credit control, answered by the logarithm method. Every rubric set needs at least one correct solution: it is easy to write a rubric that catches every mistake and also fails correct work.
case.solution: Take logs of both sides: ln y = ln(a^x) = x ln a. Differentiating implicitly, y'/y = ln a, so y' = y ln a = a^x ln(a).

case.description: Full-credit control for the other branch of the one_of group: the student rewrites a^x in exponential form and applies the chain rule instead of taking logarithms. Asserting `exponential_form` here is not over-specifying, because this solution commits to that method.
case.solution: Write y = a^x = e^{x ln a}. By the chain rule, y' = e^{x ln a} * ln a = a^x ln(a).

case.description: The misconception this question exists to catch: the student treats a^x as a power of x and applies the power rule, giving y' = x a^(x-1). `polynomial_confusion` must fire -- note that expect="fail" on a negative item means the grader identified the mistake, which is the behaviour being asserted as correct.
case.solution: Using the power rule, bring the exponent down: y' = x a^{x-1}.

case.description: Full-credit control: correct choice of u and dv, correct du and v, correct application of the formula, limits evaluated. Every rubric item should be awarded in full.
case.solution: Let u = x and dv = e^{2x} dx, so du = dx and v = (1/2) e^{2x}. Then the integral of x e^{2x} dx is x (1/2) e^{2x} - integral of (1/2) e^{2x} dx = (1/2) x e^{2x} - (1/4) e^{2x} + C = (1/4)(2x - 1) e^{2x} + C. Evaluating from 0 to 1: (1/4)(1) e^2 - (1/4)(-1) e^0 = (e^2 + 1)/4.

case.description: Correct antiderivative, then the student stops without evaluating at the limits of integration -- a definite integral answered as an indefinite one. `apply_limits` must not be awarded; the earlier items must be.
case.solution: Let u = x, dv = e^{2x} dx. Then du = dx and v = (1/2) e^{2x}, so integral of x e^{2x} dx = (1/2) x e^{2x} - (1/4) e^{2x} + C = (1/4)(2x - 1) e^{2x} + C.

case.description: The algebra slip the rubric for `correct_du_v` calls out by name: the student integrates e^{2x} to e^{2x} instead of (1/2) e^{2x}. The setup is right, so `correct_u_dv` stays at full value while `correct_du_v` loses part but not all of its credit. This case is the one that checks the rubric grants partial recognition rather than zeroing the item.
case.solution: Let u = x and dv = e^{2x} dx, so du = dx and v = e^{2x}. Then the integral is x e^{2x} - integral of e^{2x} dx = x e^{2x} - (1/2) e^{2x}, evaluated from 0 to 1, = e^2 - (1/2) e^2 + 1/2 = (e^2 + 1)/2.

case.description: Full-credit control for the two-part question. The student submits the sketch in words rather than as an image, which is what a typed submission looks like; the rubric items for part (b) should still be satisfied by an unambiguous description.
case.solution:
(a) f'(x) = e^{-x} - x e^{-x} = e^{-x}(1 - x). Since e^{-x} > 0, the only critical point with x >= 0 is x = 1, and f(1) = 1/e. So the critical point is (1, 1/e).
(b) My sketch starts at the origin, since f(0) = 0. It rises to a single maximum at (1, 1/e), which I label on the curve, and then decreases, approaching 0 from above as x goes to infinity.

case.description: The student solves f'(x) = 0 correctly but never substitutes back to get f(1) = 1/e, so part (a) is half-answered. Only part (a) is asserted on: a part with no `part` element is not checked.
case.solution: (a) f'(x) = e^{-x}(1 - x), which is zero when x = 1. So the critical point is at x = 1.
